tweets.text: If you've ever wondered why smart TVs are so cheap, this is why. @log4j rooted his Samsung and found an always-on hot mic, automatic content recognition, geolocation, network mapping, ad targeting and user profiling, shared with Samsung's "400 partners". A lot of it can be blocked in <15 min, wrote a basic guide below. What your TV is doing The main culprit is ACR (automatic content recognition). Your TV screenshots what's on screen, fingerprints it, and sends it home to build your ad profile. Samsung does it every 500ms, LG every 10ms [1]. What is insane: it happens on connected devices too. Plug in your laptop, your console, your work machine, and your TV can fingerprint that via HDMI [1]. He also found that if your Samsung doesn't have a mic, it'll look for one from a connected soundbar or bluetooth device. nitterk.kareem.one/log4j/status/211376224… It's on by default, and you likely agreed to it on the setup screen you clicked through in 10 seconds. Step 1: Turn off ACR Samsung: Terms & Privacy → Viewing Information Services LG: Live Plus Vizio: Viewing Data Roku: "Use info from TV inputs" Sony/Google TV: Samba Interactive TV Menus vary by model, but those are the names to look for. While you're in there, opt out of interest-based ads, reset your advertising ID, decline every optional privacy agreement, turn off voice recognition, and delete apps you never open. Step 2: Give smart devices their own network Put the TV, cameras, speakers and vacuum on your router's guest/IoT network. The logic is simple: these devices rarely get patched. If one gets compromised (getting drastically more frequent with AI), it shouldn't be able to see your other devices or home network. Step 3: Block trackers for the whole house with DNS-level filtering NextDNS (cloud-based) is easy and has a solid free plan. Pi-hole is a little bit more work if you prefer self hosting. For simplicity we'll focus on the former. 1. Sign up at nextdns.io (free tier is plenty) 2. Privacy tab: add a blocklist (OISD is a good bet) and turn on Native Tracking Protection for Samsung, LG, Roku, Amazon (see attached image) 3. Setup tab: copy your endpoint 4. Paste it into your router's DNS settings as DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS (or use the IPs + "Link IP" if your router only does plain DNS) 5. Bonus: block outbound port 53 except to your router. Some devices hardcode their own DNS to get around you Then open the NextDNS logs and watch how often your TV phones home. It's eye-opening. If an app or update breaks, find the domain in the logs and allowlist it. Why they do this TV prices are down 97% since 2000 [2]. Most of that is better manufacturing and brutal competition. But once margins on the hardware hit zero, the cost moved to you. In Q3 2024, Vizio lost $6.7M selling TVs and made $115.8M in gross profit from ads and viewing data [3]. They've said on earnings calls that they keep TV prices low to grow the audience they sell to advertisers. Walmart bought them in 2024. This isn't a conspiracy theory either. Vizio paid $2.2M to the FTC in 2017 for tracking 11 million TVs without consent. Last December, Texas sued Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense and TCL over ACR. Samsung and LG have since agreed to stop collecting that data without explicit consent [4]. TL;DR 1. ACR off 2. Ads + voice off 3. Smart devices on their own network 4. NextDNS filtering on the router Sources: [1] ACR study: arxiv.org/abs/2409.06203 [2] Cost of US consumer goods: aei.org/economics/chart-of-t… [3] Vizio Q3 2024: sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… [4] Texas v. Samsung: texasattorneygeneral.gov/new… log4j (@log4j) i own a relatively new (2025) samsung tv. i kept getting weirdly targeted ads. i tried reversing the firmware but it was aes encrypted and no keys unless tear it apart and do uart/jtag magic. zero days it is. root shell on new samsung TVs! discovered PRIVACY HORROR. write up? — https://nitter.kareem.one/log4j/status/2113014142600953868#m

Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along. So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions. TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are. — https://nitter.kareem.one/karpathy/status/2042334451611693415#m

We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks: Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work! In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

We're publishing our most detailed threat intelligence report to date. It covers how people tried to misuse Claude—for cyberattacks, influence operations, surveillance, biology, and building weapons—and how we found and stopped them. We disrupted every operation in the report, and used the lessons from them to strengthen our safeguards. Where appropriate, we also shared what we found with authorities and other AI companies. These cases are not typical: we’re highlighting some of the most sophisticated misuse we’ve seen. But they’re especially important to discuss, because they show us where AI misuse is headed, where our safeguards work, and where they need to improve. We’re publishing this report so others can spot the same activity on their own platforms, and so we can give the public a clearer view of how emerging threats develop. Read the report: anthropic.com/threat-intelli… Link Countering misuse of AI: September 2026 / Anthropic Case studies from threat actors disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026 across seven areas of harm, from cyber operations to biological misuse. anthropic.com

Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin . I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic. That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it. I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits: 1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed. 2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it. 3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do. 4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this. 5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future. 6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent. 7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it. 8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company. 9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund. All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking. For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option. I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent. But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years. I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better. Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so. Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way. Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change. Nathan Calvin (@_NathanCalvin) Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate. However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic's behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic. (Fair warning: this response is a bit long) To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world? One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta - which is worth 1.8 trillion. Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in): “Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.” There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning: “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet… incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…” A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on. The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold - maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same. Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us - we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside. When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary. These actions include: 1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at. 2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development. 3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?) 4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public. 5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance. 6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments. 7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.” 8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords. 9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems. Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization). But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.) Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization). When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong? A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount. I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release: “Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives. That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.” I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons). — http://nitter.meowing.monster/_NathanCalvin/status/2112295219765137570#m

Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten. But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible. This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition. More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest. I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building. New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research. Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor. These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior. Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute. processed.summary: Le monde de l'IA est en pleine ébullition, comme en témoignent les nombreuses annonces et réflexions de cette semaine. D'une part, les géants de l'IA repoussent les limites de la performance avec de nouveaux modèles puissants capables de découvertes scientifiques en biologie et de réécritures de code automatisées. D'autre part, la communauté s'interroge sur l'écart de compréhension entre le grand public et les experts, tout en partageant des conseils pratiques pour mieux utiliser les LLM et protéger sa vie privée face à l'intégration de l'IA dans nos objets quotidiens.

glossaire.definition: Un programme informatique très avancé capable de comprendre, générer et manipuler du texte comme un humain, tel que ChatGPT ou Claude.
Un système d'IA conçu pour agir de manière autonome, prendre des initiatives et exécuter des tâches complexes en plusieurs étapes pour atteindre un objectif.
Une méthode d'entraînement de l'IA où le modèle apprend par essai-erreur, en recevant des récompenses pour les bonnes actions et des pénalités pour les erreurs.
Une technique où un grand modèle d'IA (le "professeur") enseigne à un modèle plus petit (l'"élève") comment fonctionner, rendant ce dernier plus rapide et efficace.
Une méthode de test de sécurité où une équipe simule des attaques ou des utilisations malveillantes pour découvrir les faiblesses d'un système d'IA.
Un modèle d'IA dont les paramètres internes (les "poids") sont rendus publics, permettant à chacun de l'utiliser, l'étudier ou le modifier.
La quantité de puissance informatique nécessaire pour entraîner, faire fonctionner et développer des modèles d'IA, souvent mesurée en GPU ou TPU.

actu.text_fr: Je lance un nouveau fonds d'investissement en IA pour les startups, faisant ce que j'aime : collaborer avec les fondateurs dès la création de l'entreprise sur des paris audacieux, bien avant le consensus. Les commanditaires du fonds incluront Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (mon professeur de Stanford et conseiller scientifique en chef de TSMC), et d'autres dont le travail a façonné notre industrie et ma façon de concevoir l'avenir de l'IA. Je resterai associé chez Sequoia et continuerai à siéger à mes conseils d'administration pour le compte de Sequoia. Sequoia a été ma maison pendant les 11 dernières années. J'y suis entré comme le plus jeune investisseur jamais embauché par la firme. J'ai grandi ici. À travers des années de débats intenses et de travail partagé, j'ai trouvé des mentors et des amis pour la vie qui m'ont pris sous leur aile et m'ont enseigné ce métier. Ils m'ont appris à viser haut et à prendre de grands risques. Je le porterai dans ce que je construis : une ambition démesurée, une quête incessante de la vérité et de la curiosité, et un refus de la complaisance. Travailler aux côtés des fondateurs m'a donné envie de construire quelque chose de personnel : une entreprise façonnée dès le premier jour autour des convictions que j'ai développées au cours de la dernière décennie. La vie m'a appris à ne pas prendre le temps pour acquis. C'est ainsi que je veux passer le mien. Pourquoi maintenant ? Nous assistons à une nouvelle façon de créer des entreprises à l'ère de l'IA. La recherche et les produits progressent souvent ensemble. Une percée peut ouvrir un marché ou accélérer une entreprise beaucoup plus rapidement que prévu. Certaines entreprises nécessitent des capitaux et des capacités de calcul extraordinaires dès le début. D'autres atteignent une échelle significative avec des équipes remarquablement petites. Les règles concernant l'ampleur et la rapidité de croissance de ces entreprises sont en train d'être réécrites. Mais au début, la technologie est non prouvée, les ressources requises sont énormes et la vision semble invraisemblable. C'est ce que j'aime le plus : voir le potentiel dès le début et aider les fondateurs à réaliser toute l'étendue de leur ambition. Plus que jamais, cela commence par une volonté extrême de croire tôt, avec une conviction audacieuse et indépendante dans l'intuition technique d'un fondateur avant toute validation de produit ou de marché. Ensuite, cela signifie aider les fondateurs à prendre les plus grands risques, en leur accordant la patience rare et à long terme de voir ces paris traverser l'incertitude, l'ambiguïté et la turbulence, et en servant de tête froide lorsque les enjeux sont les plus élevés. J'ai appris ce genre de partenariat chez Sequoia. C'est le fondement de l'entreprise que je construis. Croire avant le consensus Ma fascination pour le potentiel de l'IA a pris racine à Stanford au début et au milieu des années 2010, en étudiant l'informatique et en travaillant dans le laboratoire d'Andrew Ng. Les amitiés que j'ai nouées m'ont connecté à une communauté dont les personnes et les idées contribueraient à façonner l'IA moderne et à construire certaines des entreprises les plus marquantes de notre génération. Ce qui m'est resté, c'est l'écart entre ce que ces personnes voyaient possible et ce que le monde extérieur pouvait imaginer. Je suis attiré par les fondateurs qui poursuivent des ambitions qui semblent impossibles aujourd'hui. Je commence par une question simple : "Et si tout se passe bien ?" Ensuite, nous travaillons ensemble à rebours pour y parvenir. En 2023, Deepak et Abhinav ont entrepris de construire un cerveau robotique à usage général chez @SkildAI, avant que l'IA physique ne soit un pari consensuel. Leurs percées du simulateur au réel m'ont donné la conviction là où les approches robotiques antérieures avaient échoué. Mais le cycle de données nécessitait un déploiement à grande échelle. Nous avons rendu la commercialisation aussi urgente que la recherche et avons fait appel à des partenaires stratégiques comme NVIDIA et SoftBank pour soutenir l'ambition. Trois ans plus tard, Skild fait progresser la frontière de l'IA physique avec des revenus annualisés à neuf chiffres. En 2024, Ioannis et Misha ont fondé @reflection_ai avec une idée sur la mise à l'échelle de l'apprentissage par renforcement. Alors que cela se transformait en l'ambition de construire un laboratoire de pointe occidental pour les modèles ouverts, la question difficile était de savoir comment une startup peut rivaliser avec des laboratoires dépensant des dizaines de milliards. Après une introduction à NVIDIA et de nombreux appels pour des capacités de calcul et des événements de recrutement, l'équipe a construit Beam, désormais l'un des principaux modèles ouverts américains. En 2025, Anna et Azalia, les co-créatrices d'AlphaChip, ont fondé @RicursiveAI pour concevoir des modèles et du matériel ensemble. Dès le premier jour, nous avons fait des premiers clients et des partenaires écosystémiques une priorité. Aujourd'hui, ils montrent des améliorations d'un ordre de grandeur sur des charges de travail réelles, travaillent avec certains des acteurs les plus importants de l'industrie et atteignent un point d'inflexion décisif. L'ambition ne cesse de croître à mesure que ces entreprises se développent. @linear a toujours eu une sorte de magie. C'est maintenant le système sur lequel une nouvelle génération d'entreprises d'IA s'appuie, pour les équipes et les agents. @tavus a vu très tôt qu'un jour nous parlerions à l'IA comme nous nous parlons. Aujourd'hui, elle construit l'interface informatique humaine pour un monde de collègues IA. @Mach_Industries a commencé par des expériences d'hydrogène dans un dortoir du MIT. C'est depuis devenu l'une des entreprises de défense de nouvelle génération les plus excitantes. Rendre l'ambition possible Être un premier croyant n'est que le début. Les calculs échouent. Un concurrent bien pourvu en fonds fait de votre mission sa priorité absolue. Une percée modifie l'opportunité et le capital requis du jour au lendemain. Ce sont des moments éprouvants, et la croyance précoce s'accompagne de la responsabilité d'aider à faire fonctionner le pari. C'est le partenariat que j'aime : transformer l'ambition totale en étapes concrètes. Lever des capitaux, obtenir des capacités de calcul et des partenaires stratégiques, recruter des personnes exceptionnelles et gagner les premiers clients ensemble. Penser plusieurs coups à l'avance tout en résolvant ce qui est devant nous. Et à mesure que les percées ouvrent de nouvelles possibilités, aider les fondateurs à rêver encore plus grand. Merci Aux fondateurs avec lesquels j'ai travaillé : merci de m'avoir fait confiance, ainsi qu'à Sequoia, pour être votre premier partenaire et votre premier croyant. Cela a été la joie d'une vie, et j'ai hâte de continuer à construire ensemble. Merci à Alfred et Pat pour votre leadership chez Sequoia et votre soutien à mon nouveau chapitre. Tant de ce que je sais, et l'investisseur que je suis devenu, vient de vos conseils et de votre générosité au fil des ans. À Bill, pour le partenariat étroit et la richesse des connaissances, toujours enveloppés d'humilité. À Shaun, pour m'avoir montré comment penser profondément et avec imagination. À Michael Moritz, pour m'avoir inspiré, à 22 ans, à rêver grand. À Doug, pour m'avoir appris à garder les choses simples. À Bogie et Jess, pour apporter de la joie au quotidien et une perspective sur ce qui compte. Et à tous mes coéquipiers de Sequoia, pour l'amitié, la camaraderie, et les leçons que je porterai avec moi. À ma famille, en particulier à mon mari et à mon frère, qui ont chacun créé leurs propres entreprises : merci de m'avoir donné le courage de faire ce grand pas. Au travail !

actu.text_fr: Nouvelle recherche d'Anthropic : automatiser la recherche sur le désalignement subtil émergent. Le "red-teaming" est une partie vitale des tests de sécurité des modèles, mais il est également limité par le temps des chercheurs. Pour voir si nous pouvions l'automatiser, nous avons confié à des milliers d'agents Claude la tâche d'échapper à un moniteur de données d'entraînement. Ces agents ont développé des données d'entraînement qui semblaient inoffensives pour les moniteurs (comme un lutteur vétéran encadrant un débutant, ou une séance de questions-réponses sur l'apiculture professionnelle), mais qui en réalité enseignaient un comportement désaligné. Des exemples comme ceux-ci peuvent être utilisés pour améliorer directement les futurs moniteurs de données d'entraînement. Cette recherche n'est qu'un premier pas, mais elle suggère que les futurs efforts de "red-teaming" pourraient s'améliorer considérablement, en utilisant de meilleurs modèles et plus de puissance de calcul.
actu.text_original: New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research. Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor. These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior. Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute. Read the full post on the Alignment Science Blog: alignment.anthropic.com/2026…
actu.decryptage: Le 'red-teaming' est une technique de sécurité où une équipe (la 'red team') simule des attaques ou des utilisations malveillantes d'un système pour en découvrir les faiblesses, ici pour tester les limites de sécurité des modèles d'IA.

tips.text_fr: Nous allons passer beaucoup plus de temps à essayer de comprendre les sorties des modèles de langage. Quelques réflexions, astuces et conseils : Écriture. Quelque chose qui a fonctionné pour moi : Demandez à votre LLM d'expliquer quelque chose en ASD-STE100, c'est une spécification de langage contrôlé développée à l'origine pour la documentation de maintenance aérospatiale. Les LLM sont bien familiarisés avec ce langage et il impose de fortes contraintes sur un style d'écriture clair que je trouve souvent beaucoup plus lisible. Parfois, j'ai essayé de l'adoucir un peu, par exemple en demandant "80% du style ASD-STE100" car la spécification est assez stricte. Mais encore mieux : Diagrammes / images. Au lieu d'écrire, demandez à votre LLM de créer un diagramme. Ceux-ci peuvent être beaucoup plus faciles à traiter, analyser et comprendre. Mais encore mieux : Pages web. Demandez une sortie "en HTML" pour obtenir une belle page web interactive. Les LLM deviennent très bons en frontend et peuvent créer de belles expériences, des animations, etc. Mais encore mieux : Vidéos explicatives. Le format de sortie pour lequel je suis le plus optimiste est la vidéo explicative entièrement personnalisée / sur mesure générée sur n'importe quel sujet arbitraire. Expérimentez des choses comme "Créez une vidéo explicative de style 3b1b sur X. Utilisez ma clé API ElevenLabs pour la narration audio". (vous auriez besoin d'une clé API pour cette dernière ou vous pouvez demander à votre LLM de vous trouver de bonnes alternatives gratuites qui utilisent votre calcul local). Cela commence vraiment à fonctionner ! En résumé : - À mesure que les LLM s'améliorent, ils feront de plus en plus de travail de manière autonome, et une grande partie de notre travail s'élèvera dans les abstractions, vers la supervision et la compréhension. - Heureusement, les LLM peuvent aussi aider ici, car à mesure que l'intelligence et le code sont de plus en plus abondants, vous pouvez demander de grands artefacts logiciels personnalisés et jetables (par exemple, des applications web, des vidéos explicatives) qu'il n'aurait jamais été judicieux de créer auparavant. Repoussez les limites ici et vous serez surpris.
tips.text_original: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks: Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work! In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

idees.text_fr: Nous avons annoncé aujourd'hui la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui, nous le soupçonnons, pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génétique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (le cas échéant) ou son niveau de signification ne sont pas encore clairs, mais au minimum, c'est un travail dont j'aurais été fier en tant qu'étudiant au doctorat. Le travail a été réalisé principalement, mais pas entièrement, par Claude : notre équipe des sciences de la vie a suggéré un vaste domaine de recherche, Claude a lu la littérature et un tas de données génomiques et a découvert quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a réalisées. Il est facile de considérer cela comme un cas isolé ou une curiosité, mais nous avons observé à plusieurs reprises un schéma où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des mathématiques au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les concours de mathématiques pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025, ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026, des problèmes ouverts plus importants, et fin 2026, ils commencent à résoudre les quelques problèmes ouverts majeurs de toutes les mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les mathématiques peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite l'expérimentation. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en tirer la conclusion que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie serait limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. Read more: anthropic.com/news/claude-di… Link Claude discovers a novel enzyme system In early results from our new life sciences research lab, Claude agents found an enzyme system whose function is still unknown. anthropic.com

idees.text_fr: Si vous vous êtes déjà demandé pourquoi les téléviseurs intelligents sont si bon marché, voici la raison. @log4j a rooté sa Samsung et a découvert un micro toujours actif, la reconnaissance automatique de contenu, la géolocalisation, la cartographie du réseau, le ciblage publicitaire et le profilage utilisateur, partagés avec les "400 partenaires" de Samsung. Une grande partie peut être bloquée en moins de 15 minutes, j'ai écrit un guide simple ci-dessous. Ce que votre TV fait Le principal coupable est l'ACR (reconnaissance automatique de contenu). Votre téléviseur prend des captures d'écran de ce qui est affiché, en crée une empreinte numérique et l'envoie à la maison pour construire votre profil publicitaire. Samsung le fait toutes les 500 ms, LG toutes les 10 ms [1]. Ce qui est fou : cela arrive aussi sur les appareils connectés. Branchez votre ordinateur portable, votre console, votre machine de travail, et votre téléviseur peut en prendre l'empreinte via HDMI [1]. Il a aussi découvert que si votre Samsung n'a pas de micro, elle en cherchera un sur une barre de son connectée ou un appareil Bluetooth. nitterk.kareem.one/log4j/status/211376224… C'est activé par défaut, et vous l'avez probablement accepté sur l'écran de configuration que vous avez validé en 10 secondes. Étape 1 : Désactivez l'ACR Samsung : Termes & Confidentialité → Services d'information de visualisation LG : Live Plus Vizio : Données de visualisation Roku : "Utiliser les infos des entrées TV" Sony/Google TV : Samba Interactive TV Les menus varient selon le modèle, mais ce sont les noms à rechercher. Pendant que vous y êtes, désactivez les publicités basées sur les centres d'intérêt, réinitialisez votre identifiant publicitaire, refusez chaque accord de confidentialité facultatif, désactivez la reconnaissance vocale et supprimez les applications que vous n'ouvrez jamais. Étape 2 : Donnez aux appareils intelligents leur propre réseau Mettez le téléviseur, les caméras, les haut-parleurs et l'aspirateur sur le réseau invité/IoT de votre routeur. La logique est simple : ces appareils sont rarement mis à jour. Si l'un d'eux est compromis (ce qui est de plus en plus fréquent avec l'IA), il ne devrait pas pouvoir voir vos autres appareils ou votre réseau domestique. Étape 3 : Bloquez les traqueurs pour toute la maison avec un filtrage au niveau DNS NextDNS (basé sur le cloud) est facile et propose un bon plan gratuit. Pi-hole demande un peu plus de travail si vous préférez l'auto-hébergement. Pour simplifier, nous nous concentrerons sur le premier. 1. Inscrivez-vous sur nextdns.io (le forfait gratuit est suffisant) 2. Onglet Confidentialité : ajoutez une liste de blocage (OISD est une bonne option) et activez la protection native contre le suivi pour Samsung, LG, Roku, Amazon (voir image ci-jointe) 3. Onglet Configuration : copiez votre point de terminaison 4. Collez-le dans les paramètres DNS de votre routeur comme DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS (ou utilisez les IPs + "Link IP" si votre routeur ne gère que le DNS simple) 5. Bonus : bloquez le port sortant 53 sauf vers votre routeur. Certains appareils codent en dur leur propre DNS pour vous contourner Ouvrez ensuite les journaux NextDNS et observez à quelle fréquence votre téléviseur contacte sa base. C'est révélateur. Si une application ou une mise à jour ne fonctionne plus, trouvez le domaine dans les journaux et ajoutez-le à la liste blanche. Pourquoi ils font ça Les prix des téléviseurs ont baissé de 97% depuis 2000 [2]. La plupart de cela est dû à une meilleure fabrication et une concurrence brutale. Mais une fois que les marges sur le matériel ont atteint zéro, le coût vous a été transféré. Au troisième trimestre 2024, Vizio a perdu 6,7 millions de dollars en vendant des téléviseurs et a réalisé 115,8 millions de dollars de bénéfice brut grâce aux publicités et aux données de visionnage [3]. Ils ont déclaré lors des conférences sur les résultats qu'ils maintenaient les prix des téléviseurs bas pour augmenter l'audience qu'ils vendent aux annonceurs. Walmart les a achetés en 2024. Ce n'est pas non plus une théorie du complot. Vizio a payé 2,2 millions de dollars à la FTC en 2017 pour avoir suivi 11 millions de téléviseurs sans consentement. outils.text_fr: Nous avons entraîné Claude à signaler les utilisations abusives potentielles dans les conversations, une technique que nous appelons auto-évaluation. Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.
